spatial_claims.claim: F is diametrically opposite A on the circle, with AF a diameter passing through center O
Five equal arcs of 72 degrees each; central angle AOB = 72 degrees
M is the midpoint of arc AB, so central angle AOM = 36 degrees
OA and OF are opposite rays, so angle BOF = 180 - 72 = 108 degrees
Triangle BOF is isosceles (OB = OF = r) with base angles OBF = OFB = 36 degrees
BF > BO since BF is opposite the larger angle (108 > 36)
T lies between B and F on segment BF with BT = BO = r
Triangle BOT is isosceles with angle BOT = angle OTB = 72 degrees
Angle BOF = angle BOT + angle TOF, so angle TOF = 108 - 72 = 36 degrees (ray OT between rays OB and OF)
Angle OFT = angle OFB = 36 degrees (same angle since T on BF), so triangle OTF is isosceles with TF = OT
SAS congruence: triangles BOT and OAM with BO = OA = r, BT = OM = r, included angles both 36 degrees, giving OT = AM = d
BF = BT + TF = r + d (additive since T between B and F)
Angle ABF = 90 degrees (angle in semicircle since AF is diameter and B on circle)

configuration_map: O is the center of the circle throughout. A and B are adjacent pentagon vertices on the circle. F is on the circle diametrically opposite A, making AF a diameter through O; F is used consistently in this role in all steps. M is on the circle at the midpoint of arc AB, used only in the SAS congruence in Step 5 as a vertex of triangle OAM. T is constructed on segment BF (between B and F) with BT = r; it serves as the vertex of triangles BOT and OTF. The ray OT falls between rays OB and OF because T is interior to segment BF and O is off line BF, making the angle decomposition BOF = BOT + TOF valid. The supplementary angles at T (OTB = 72, OTF = 108) are consistent with T being on line BF.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent. The key angle decomposition (angle BOF = angle BOT + angle TOF) is valid because T lies between B and F, placing ray OT between rays OB and OF. The SAS congruence is correctly set up with matching sides and included angles. The right angle at B from the semicircle theorem is properly applied. The proof takes a different but geometrically sound route from Heath, using an auxiliary point T on BF and a congruence argument to establish BF = r + d, then algebraic manipulation to reach the result.
